extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court justices and patent-law practitioners (patent litigators and judges)
extracted.subtask_description: A Supreme Court certiorari petition arguing legal standards for Section 101 patent eligibility of computer-implemented inventions, criticizing Federal Circuit application of Alice/Mayo and urging clarification of when software/file-system inventions are patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Two steps: (i) in step one, 'determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of [the] patent-ineligible concepts;' and (ii) in step two, 'ask, [w]hat else is there in the claims before us?' (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217-218). The Court described step two as a search for 'an element or combination of elements that is sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [concept] itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use step one to identify whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea); use step two to search for 'additional elements' that transform the claim into 'significantly more.' Both steps involve looking at claim elements both individually and in combination. Examples and citations: Alice; Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claims 'as a whole' (Diehr principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Diehr, claims 'must be considered as a whole' and courts should not 'dissect' claims into new and old elements and ignore the old elements in the eligibility analysis. (Diehr, 450 U.S. at 188.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying § 101, evaluate the claimed invention in its entirety rather than breaking it into constituent steps and treating some as 'ineligible' and discarding them. The petition criticizes lower courts that analyze individual steps separately instead of the whole-claim perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of inventions historically held 'abstract ideas'
rubrics_metrics.description: In fifty years of jurisprudence, this Court has only ever held two types of inventions patent-ineligible as directed to an 'abstract idea:' (i) business methods (Bilski, Alice); and (ii) mathematical algorithms (Benson, Flook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these historical categories to limit the scope of the judicial exception: do not expand 'abstract idea' beyond business methods and mathematical algorithms without clear justification from precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-improvement test from Alice
rubrics_metrics.description: In Alice, the Court said inventions that 'improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'effect an improvement in any other technology or technical field' should be patent-eligible. (Alice, 573 U.S. at 225.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that effect a technical improvement to computer functionality or another technical field should be treated as eligible; show how claimed features solve a problem specifically arising in the technical realm and materially improve functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: DDR test — 'necessarily rooted in computer technology'
rubrics_metrics.description: DDR Holdings articulated that a computer invention is eligible if 'the claimed solution is necessarily rooted in computer technology in order to overcome a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks.' (DDR, 773 F.3d at 1255-59.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this test to ask whether the claimed solution inherently requires computer technology to solve a computer-specific problem (example: fusing website 'look and feel' with third-party content). The petition notes this test was an early Federal Circuit attempt to cabin eligibility for software claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enfish test — 'specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities'
rubrics_metrics.description: Enfish held that eligibility turns on whether 'the focus of the claims is on the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities … or, instead, on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.' (Enfish, 822 F.3d at 1335-36.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to distinguish claims that improve computer capabilities (eligible) from those that merely use a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea (ineligible). The petition criticizes this distinction as subjective and panel-dependent in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct identification of the 'abstract idea' (proper level of abstraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'abstract idea' must be defined at the correct level — neither too broad nor too narrow. The petition criticizes the Federal Circuit for (a) treating concrete computer steps as 'abstract' and (b) failing to recognize the key, technology-specific benefits (e.g., MD functions providing virtually unique identifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying the purported abstract idea, account for the invention's technical features and benefits (credit what the MD/hash provides) rather than collapsing claims to overly generalized analogies (e.g., library call numbers). Define the abstract idea consistent with Benson/Flook (e.g., the message-digest algorithm itself when that is the mathematical feature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'read out' ineligible elements at Alice step two
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper, at step two, to read the elements deemed 'abstract ideas' out of the claim and search for an 'inventive concept' only among the remaining elements; claims must be considered as an 'ordered combination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an 'inventive concept' exists by considering all claim elements in combination, including those that relate to the judicial exception. The petition identifies cases (e.g., BSG) where courts dissected claims and disregarded ineligible elements, resulting in erroneous invalidations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into specific technical operations ('significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that integrates a mathematical computation into specific, useful computer operations that produce useful results recites 'significantly more' than the algorithm itself (Diehr analogy). Claims that merely claim the algorithm in the abstract are more likely ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the mathematical/algorithmic element is tied to concrete implementation steps that effect a technological improvement (examples: using MD values to control authorization, to store/retrieve files, and to deduplicate files). Distinguish from claims that only add 'insignificant pre- or post-solution activity' (Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not 'wholly preempt' the underlying algorithm; uses of the algorithm outside the specific claimed application should remain open (Flook concern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed invention precludes all uses of the underlying mathematical tool. If the claim is limited to a specific application or technical environment, preemption concerns are reduced and eligibility support increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two involves underlying factual questions (Berkheimer/Aatrix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized that Alice step two can involve underlying factual issues. These factual disputes must be credited for the non-movant on motions to dismiss (Rule 12(c)), and genuine disputes of fact should preclude dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the presence of an 'inventive concept' depends on factual matters (e.g., whether elements are 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' or whether a feature provides a technical advantage), courts should not resolve eligibility on the pleadings; summary judgment or trial may be required. The petition notes lower courts frequently ignore this despite Berkheimer/Aatrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete computer operations are not necessarily 'abstract'
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete computer steps — e.g., 'comparing that content-based identifier' (CPU processing) or 'providing/denying access to, or deleting data' (physically transports or modifies data) — are not the sorts of things this Court has held to be 'abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat routine data-processing, physical data transport, or other concrete computer operations as abstract ideas absent precedent; these operations may indicate a technical improvement rather than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions confined to fundamental building blocks, not technological developments
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial exceptions to patentability are intended to exclude only 'fundamental building blocks of human ingenuity' (such as a pure mathematical computation), not new developments in computer or other technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the scope of judicial exceptions to basic tools of innovation. Novel applications or improvements in computer technology (e.g., new file-system architectures using hashes) should not be swept into the exception merely because they involve mathematical operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for objective, consistent standards (avoid panel-dependent subjectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility jurisprudence should provide predictable, objective standards rather than 'panel-dependent' subjective distinctions that allow similar claims to be alternately held eligible or ineligible based on judicial composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear, consistent tests (e.g., affirming 'claims as a whole' approach, clarifying what counts as 'technical improvement') to avoid inconsistent outcomes across panels and cases (examples of contradictory Federal Circuit outcomes are provided).
